title: Cosmology III: physical and observational cosmology
scope: The real universe and the evidence for its contents and history, taking the Robertson-Walker kinematics and Friedmann dynamics as given: standard candles, magnitudes and the cosmic distance ladder, Type Ia supernovae and the discovery of accelerating expansion, dark energy and its alternatives, the observational case for dark matter and its candidates, the hot big bang and thermal history (radiation era, matter-radiation equality, phase transitions, photon-to-baryon ratio, baryon asymmetry), big bang nucleosynthesis and the baryon density, recombination and the cosmic microwave background with its dipole, anisotropies, angular power spectrum, polarization and E/B modes, baryon acoustic oscillations, Lambda-CDM and the Hubble tension, structure formation from density perturbations to first stars and reionization, and inflation (horizon and flatness problems, inflaton, Hubble friction, slow roll, reheating, primordial perturbations and gravitational waves), plus cosmic strings as early-universe relics.

concepts.title: Olbers' paradox
concepts.summary: If the universe were infinite, eternal, static and uniformly filled with stars, every line of sight would end on a stellar surface and the night sky would blaze. The dark sky is explained mainly by the finite age of the universe, which limits how far light has travelled to us, with cosmological redshift dimming distant sources further.
concepts.notes: DIV works through the equal-intensity-shell argument and several variants and rejected resolutions (absorbing dust, hierarchies).

concepts.title: Uniqueness of the universe
concepts.summary: Cosmology studies a single object that cannot be repeated or experimented on, so its models rest on extrapolating locally tested physics together with simplifying assumptions such as the cosmological principle. This limits what can be tested statistically and explains why symmetry postulates play such a large role.

concepts.title: Apparent magnitude and distance modulus
concepts.summary: Astronomers measure brightness on a reversed logarithmic scale, m = constant - 2.5 log10(flux), so fainter objects have larger magnitudes; the difference between apparent and absolute magnitude, m - M, is the distance modulus, a logarithm of the luminosity distance. The reversed sign and the factor 2.5 are common sources of confusion.

concepts.title: Standard candle
concepts.summary: A class of astronomical sources whose intrinsic luminosity is known from physics or from calibration, so that the measured flux gives the luminosity distance. Any evolution of the class over cosmic time biases the distances, which is why ordinary galaxies make poor candles.
concepts.notes: Galaxy evolution (DIV ch24) is folded in as the reason galaxies cannot serve as standard candles: distant galaxies are seen younger and need not share the luminosity of nearby ones.

concepts.title: Cepheid period-luminosity relation
concepts.summary: Cepheid variable stars pulsate with periods tightly correlated with their average luminosity, a relation Henrietta Leavitt found from stars at a common distance in the Magellanic Clouds. Once calibrated by parallax, measuring a Cepheid's period gives its luminosity and hence its distance.
concepts.notes: SCH notes a possible weak dependence on chemical composition as a systematic.

concepts.title: Cosmic distance ladder
concepts.summary: Distances to far objects are built in overlapping steps: geometric parallax fixes nearby stars, which calibrate Cepheids, which calibrate brighter indicators such as Type Ia supernovae in more distant galaxies. Each rung inherits the systematic errors of the rungs beneath it.

names: tip of the red giant branch

merged_from: tip of the red giant branch
concepts.notes: The tip of the red giant branch (SCH ch13, mention) is folded in as an alternative calibrator rung based on the maximum luminosity of red giants.

concepts.title: Type Ia supernova
concepts.summary: A white dwarf, typically fed by a companion, ignites runaway carbon burning near the Chandrasekhar mass and is completely disrupted. Because the progenitor mass is nearly fixed, peak luminosities are similar (and standardizable), making these explosions bright standard candles visible to redshifts of order one.

concepts.title: Magnitude-redshift (Hubble) diagram
concepts.summary: A plot of distance modulus against redshift for standard candles: the low-redshift slope measures the Hubble constant, and the curvature of the relation near z of order one measures the deceleration parameter and so whether expansion is speeding up. To first order beyond linear, the correction term is proportional to (1 - q0) z.

concepts.title: Dimensionless Hubble constant (little h)
concepts.summary: Writing H0 = 100 h km/s/Mpc (or H0 = 70 h_70 km/s/Mpc) lets formulas carry the uncertainty in the Hubble constant as an explicit factor; h is about 0.7. The symbol h must not be confused with a gravitational-wave strain amplitude or with Planck's constant.
concepts.notes: GA uses the 100 km/s/Mpc normalization, SCH the 70 km/s/Mpc normalization; both are the same convention.

concepts.title: Accelerating expansion of the universe
aliases: positive second derivative of the scale factor
concepts.summary: Type Ia supernova surveys in 1998-99, later confirmed by the CMB and galaxy surveys, showed that distant supernovae are fainter than a decelerating universe allows, so the expansion rate is increasing today. By the acceleration equation this requires a dominant component with pressure below minus one third of its energy density.
concepts.notes: GA ch41 uses the kinematic condition (second derivative of a positive) mainly to set up inflation; that condition is included here, while its use for the early universe lives under cosmic-inflation. The legacy distance lab proposed a supernova-data fit reproducing this inference.

concepts.title: Dark energy
concepts.summary: Dark energy is the name for whatever drives the present acceleration and makes up roughly 70 per cent of the cosmic energy budget. In its simplest form it is a cosmological constant, a fluid with constant density and pressure equal to minus that density, but it could instead be vacuum energy, an evolving scalar field, or a sign that gravity is modified on large scales.
concepts.notes: DIV ch01 names dark matter and dark energy together; that cluster is split between dark-energy and dark-matter. DIV stresses the two readings of Lambda (geometric term on the left, vacuum fluid on the right). The legacy course emphasises that dark matter and dark energy play distinct explanatory roles.

concepts.title: Quintessence
concepts.summary: An alternative to a strict cosmological constant in which dark energy is a slowly rolling scalar field, so its density and equation-of-state parameter can change with time. It uses the same scalar-field machinery as inflation, applied to the late universe.

concepts.title: Averaging problem in cosmology
concepts.summary: Because the Einstein equations are nonlinear, the spacetime produced by a smoothed-out matter distribution need not equal the average of the true lumpy spacetime. Fitting a Robertson-Walker model to an inhomogeneous universe could therefore bias inferred parameters, a possible loophole in the inference of dark energy.

concepts.title: Temperature-redshift relation
concepts.summary: Radiation energy density falls as a^-4 and a black body has energy density proportional to T^4, so the radiation temperature scales as 1/a: T = T0 (1 + z). The universe was a thousand times hotter when it was a thousand times smaller, which makes temperature a clock for the early universe.
concepts.notes: DIV singles this out as one of the two results to retain from its Level 2 material. Handed over from cosmological-kinematics.

concepts.title: Hot big bang model
concepts.summary: The picture in which the universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense state and cooled as it grew, since radiation temperature falls inversely with the scale factor; as it cooled, nuclei, then atoms, then stars and galaxies formed. Its pillars are the Hubble expansion, the cosmic microwave background and the light-element abundances.
concepts.notes: The classical singularity itself (a = 0) belongs to cosmological-dynamics as big-bang-singularity; this concept is the physical model of a hot early universe.

concepts.title: Cosmic microwave background
concepts.summary: Nearly perfect black-body radiation at 2.725 K that fills the universe, released when the early plasma became neutral and transparent and redshifted by a factor of about 1100 since. Predicted by Alpher and Herman and found by Penzias and Wilson, it is the key evidence for a hot big bang, shows isotropy to about one part in 100,000, and fixes the radiation density.
concepts.notes: SCH also uses the CMB operationally to define the cosmic rest frame and constant-time slices. Misconception to address: the CMB does not come from a physical shell or edge (see last-scattering-surface).

concepts.title: Preservation of the black-body spectrum under expansion
concepts.summary: As the universe expands every photon frequency falls as 1/a, and a thermal spectrum stays exactly thermal with a temperature that also falls as 1/a, because the ratio of photon energy to temperature is unchanged and the frequency-cubed factor dilutes exactly like inverse volume. This is why radiation released at decoupling is still a near-perfect black body today.

names: preservation of the black-body form under expansion

merged_from: preservation of the black-body form under expansion

concepts.title: CMB dipole and the cosmic rest frame
concepts.summary: Our motion relative to the frame in which the CMB is isotropic Doppler-shifts it into a dipole pattern, slightly hotter ahead and cooler behind; Planck finds the Solar System moving at about 370 km/s. The CMB frame is physically distinguished by the matter content of the universe, though not privileged by the laws of physics.

names: CMB rest frame and dipole anisotropy

merged_from: CMB rest frame and dipole anisotropy

concepts.title: Thermal history of the universe
concepts.summary: Because temperature scales as 1/a, the early universe can be labelled by temperature or typical particle energy instead of time, and read as a sequence: free quarks, then free nucleons, nuclei in a radiation-dominated plasma, a matter-dominated plasma, and finally neutral atoms with free-streaming light. Physics at each stage is set by which reactions are fast compared with the expansion, and the picture is laboratory-tested up to about TeV energies.
concepts.notes: DIV ch25 gives the broader qualitative sequence inflation, radiation (t^1/2), matter (t^2/3), vacuum (de Sitter); it is folded in here. DIV tabulates the thermal epochs in its Table 26.2. The radiation-dominated solution itself is cosmological-dynamics/radiation-dominated-universe.

concepts.title: Temperature-time relation in the radiation era
concepts.summary: During radiation domination a grows as t^(1/2) and T falls as 1/a, so T is proportional to t^(-1/2); numerically the temperature is about 10^10 K, or roughly 1 MeV, when the universe is one second old. This turns the thermal history into a clock for nuclear and particle processes.

names: temperature-time relation in the radiation era

merged_from: temperature-time relation in the radiation era

concepts.title: Matter-radiation equality
concepts.summary: Radiation density falls as a^-4 and matter density as a^-3, so they were equal when the scale factor was the present ratio of radiation to matter density parameters, about 3 x 10^-4 of today (redshift of a few thousand, tens of thousands of years after the big bang). Before it the expansion was radiation-dominated, after it matter-dominated, which changes both a(t) and how structure grows.
concepts.notes: The two books use slightly different radiation densities, so quoted equality times differ by an order of magnitude; the scale-factor ratio is the robust statement.

concepts.title: Phase transitions in the early universe
concepts.summary: As the hot universe cooled it is thought to have passed through symmetry-changing transitions: separation of the strong force near 10^15 GeV, electroweak symmetry breaking by the Higgs field near 100 GeV, and confinement of quarks into hadrons at a few hundred MeV, around 10^-5 to 10^-4 s. Before confinement matter was a quark-gluon plasma.

names: phase transitions in the early Universe

merged_from: phase transitions in the early Universe
concepts.notes: The temperature-dependent effective potential used by GA to model the transition belongs to action-principles-and-field-theory.

concepts.title: Cosmic string
concepts.summary: A hypothetical line-like topological defect formed in an early-universe symmetry-breaking transition and stretched to astronomical length. It has tension equal to its mass per unit length, leaves flat space around it with a missing wedge (deficit angle) that would create double images, and its oscillations and cusps would emit gravitational-wave bursts.

names: gravitational lensing by a cosmic string

merged_from: gravitational lensing by a cosmic string
concepts.notes: None has been observed; SCH mentions routine gravitational-wave burst searches for string cusps. Lensing by a straight string (two identical undistorted images from the deficit angle, GA ch49) is folded in.

concepts.title: Photon-to-baryon ratio
concepts.summary: There are roughly a billion photons for every baryon in the universe, a number fixed after electron-positron pairs annihilated at around one second and conserved since; it measures the entropy per particle. Its size explains why rare high-energy photons could keep hydrogen ionized until the temperature fell well below the ionization energy.
concepts.notes: Electron-positron annihilation near kT ~ 500 keV is folded in as the event that fixes the ratio.

concepts.title: Matter-antimatter asymmetry
concepts.summary: The present universe contains essentially no antimatter, so the early plasma must have held a tiny excess of matter, about one extra particle per billion photons, which survived annihilation. Producing it (baryogenesis) requires baryon-number, C and CP violation out of equilibrium, and its cause is still unknown.

concepts.title: Big bang nucleosynthesis
concepts.summary: In the first few minutes, as the plasma cooled through tens of keV, protons and neutrons fused into deuterium, helium-4 (about a quarter by mass), helium-3 and lithium-7, while expansion shut reactions off before heavier nuclei formed. The yields depend on the baryon density and expansion rate, so matching observed abundances fixes the baryon density parameter at about 0.04-0.05.
concepts.notes: An independent check of the baryon density against the CMB; stars destroy rather than create deuterium, so its abundance is primordial.

concepts.title: Nucleosynthesis bound on relativistic species
concepts.summary: Extra massless particle species would add energy density, speed up the early expansion and raise the helium yield, so observed abundances limit the number of light neutrino families to the known three. The same argument bounds any early background of relativistic energy, including primordial gravitational waves, and requires dark matter to have been non-relativistic.

concepts.title: Baryon density parameter
concepts.summary: The fraction of the critical density in ordinary matter made of protons, neutrons and electrons, about 0.04-0.05 from nucleosynthesis and the CMB. It is several times the matter in visible stars but only about a sixth of the total matter density, showing that most ordinary matter is dark and most matter is not baryonic.

concepts.title: Galaxy rotation curve
concepts.summary: The orbital speed of stars and gas plotted against distance from a galaxy's centre. Newtonian circular orbits predict speeds falling as r^(-1/2) outside the visible mass, but observed curves stay roughly flat, implying enclosed mass growing in proportion to r in an unseen halo.

concepts.title: Dark matter
concepts.summary: Matter that emits no light and is detected only by its gravity, through cluster dynamics (Zwicky), flat galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing and structure formation; it forms extended halos around galaxies and makes up about 85 per cent of all matter. Nucleosynthesis shows it cannot be ordinary baryons, and the favoured cold form moves slowly compared with light, but its particle nature is unknown.
concepts.notes: SCH gives the evidence its own subsection (Zwicky's Coma cluster virial analysis, Rubin's rotation curves, cluster lensing); folded in here. GA ch18's missing mass problem is the historical framing (visible matter far below critical density). The dark matter halo (SCH mention) is the extended distribution around galaxies.

concepts.title: Dark matter candidates
concepts.summary: Proposals for what dark matter is: astrophysical objects such as primordial black holes or massive compact halo objects (limited by microlensing), light neutrinos (too hot to build structure), and new particles such as axions or weakly interacting massive particles sought in direct-detection and collider experiments. None has been confirmed.
concepts.notes: Primordial black holes as objects are owned by black-holes; they appear here only as a candidate. GA ch49 mentions supersymmetry as a possible source.

concepts.title: Recombination and photon decoupling
concepts.summary: About 380,000 years after the big bang (redshift about 1100, temperature about 3000 K) the plasma cooled enough for electrons to bind into neutral hydrogen, photons stopped scattering, and the universe became transparent, releasing the CMB. It happened far below the 13.6 eV ionization energy because the huge number of photons per baryon kept the gas ionized until then.
concepts.notes: Strictly, recombination (atoms forming) slightly precedes photon decoupling; the books treat them as one epoch. SCH calls the resulting limit on electromagnetic observation the optical horizon (received here from black-holes).

concepts.title: Last scattering surface
concepts.summary: The sphere around a given observer made of the points where the CMB photons now reaching that observer last scattered at decoupling. It is not a physical shell: light was released everywhere, and observers at other places or times see different spheres.

concepts.title: CMB temperature anisotropies
concepts.summary: After removing the dipole, the CMB temperature varies across the sky by about one part in 100,000, tracing density and velocity perturbations at decoupling. The positions of hot and cold spots are random, but their typical size as a function of angular scale is fixed by early-universe physics and cosmological parameters.

concepts.title: CMB angular power spectrum
aliases: multipole expansion of the CMB sky
concepts.summary: Expanding the sky temperature in spherical harmonics, with multipole l corresponding to angular scale of roughly 180 degrees divided by l, and averaging the squared coefficients at each l gives the power spectrum. Its series of acoustic peaks, the first near l of about 200, encodes spatial curvature and the baryon, dark matter and dark energy content.

names: multipole expansion of the CMB sky
CMB anisotropies and angular power spectrum

merged_from: CMB anisotropies and angular power spectrum
multipole expansion of the CMB sky
concepts.notes: SCH notes that the phases of the multipole coefficients carry the random positions of spots while their squared amplitudes carry the physics; DIV uses the equivalent angular correlation function. Relies on spherical harmonics, which no mathematics concept yet registers; add the prerequisite when one exists.

concepts.title: Baryon acoustic oscillations
concepts.summary: Before decoupling, pressure waves travelled through the tightly coupled baryon-photon plasma, and the distance they covered by then is imprinted both on the CMB peaks and as a preferred separation of about 150 Mpc in today's galaxy distribution. This known physical length acts as a standard ruler for angular-diameter distances and the expansion history.
concepts.notes: Photon drag (the coupling of baryons to photons until the drag epoch; received from matter-and-stress-energy) is folded in as the mechanism that sustains the oscillations. The legacy research-window card warns that joint BAO fits hinting at evolving dark energy are not established results.

concepts.title: CMB polarization
concepts.summary: Scattering off electrons polarizes light perpendicular to the plane of scattering; isotropic incident light cancels, but radiation brighter from some directions than others (a quadrupole pattern around the scatterer) leaves net linear polarization. The CMB is therefore weakly polarized in a pattern tied to its anisotropies at last scattering.

concepts.title: Lambda-CDM model
concepts.summary: The standard cosmological model: a spatially flat Friedmann-Robertson-Walker universe with about 5 per cent baryons, 26 per cent cold dark matter and 69 per cent cosmological constant, plus a little radiation, starting hot and probably preceded by inflation. Once radiation is negligible its scale factor goes from t^(2/3) deceleration to exponential acceleration, and it fits the CMB, supernovae, BAO and nucleosynthesis with an age of about 13.8 billion years.
concepts.notes: SCH justifies the "cold" by simulations: dark matter with low random velocities lets overdense regions collapse in time to trap baryons. GA frames the modern parameter-measurement era as precision cosmology. DIV gives the exact matter-plus-Lambda solution a ∝ sinh^(2/3)(t/t_Lambda).

concepts.title: Hubble tension
concepts.summary: Local distance-ladder measurements give a Hubble constant near 73-74 km/s/Mpc, while fitting Lambda-CDM to the CMB with BAO gives about 67, a disagreement of several standard deviations. It may come from unrecognised systematics in either method or signal missing physics, and standard sirens offer an independent arbiter.
concepts.notes: Quoted values are dated (SCH cites mid-2021 numbers); refresh when authoring.

concepts.title: Growth of density perturbations
concepts.summary: Slightly overdense regions pull in matter and grow denser while underdense regions empty, but expansion slows the runaway: in a matter-dominated Einstein-de Sitter universe the linear density contrast grows only as t^(2/3), or in proportion to the scale factor. Simulations reproduce observed galaxy clustering from the small CMB-era perturbations only when dark matter is included.

names: growth of density perturbations in an expanding universe

merged_from: growth of density perturbations in an expanding universe
concepts.notes: GA treats it as an exercise with Newtonian fluid equations in comoving coordinates (growing t^(2/3) and decaying 1/t modes).

concepts.title: Radiative cooling of baryons in dark matter halos
concepts.summary: After decoupling, gas falling into dark matter wells is heated by collisions and radiates the energy away; losing energy makes the gas sink deeper and, because self-gravitating systems have negative specific heat, get hotter, so baryons concentrate at the centre. Collisionless dark matter cannot radiate and stays in extended halos.

names: radiative cooling of baryons in dark matter wells

merged_from: radiative cooling of baryons in dark matter wells

concepts.title: Hierarchical structure formation
concepts.summary: In Lambda-CDM small clumps collapse first and then merge repeatedly into larger galaxies and clusters, a process that continues today (the Milky Way will merge with Andromeda). Because stars are nearly collisionless, groups accreted together stay coherent streams in position-velocity space, and Gaia velocities reveal the Galaxy's merger history.

names: galactic stellar streams and phase-space conservation

merged_from: galactic stellar streams and phase-space conservation
concepts.notes: Galactic stellar streams and Liouville phase-space conservation (received from matter-and-stress-energy) are folded in as the observational archaeology of mergers.

concepts.title: Population III stars
concepts.summary: The first generation of stars, formed from pristine hydrogen and helium; without heavy elements the gas was transparent and cooled poorly, so they were very massive, hot and short-lived, enriched their surroundings with metals and probably left many black holes. None has yet been observed directly.

concepts.title: Reionization and the cosmic dark ages
concepts.summary: After decoupling the universe was neutral and nearly lightless (the dark ages) until ultraviolet light from the first stars and galaxies ionized intergalactic hydrogen again, between redshifts of roughly 20 and 8. Light from the dark ages was largely absorbed, but low-frequency radio and gravitational waves pass through, so detectors such as LISA may see black-hole mergers from that time.

concepts.title: Horizon problem
concepts.summary: In a decelerating hot big bang, the past light cones of points on opposite sides of the last scattering surface never overlap, so nothing could have brought them to a common temperature; only patches within about two degrees on today's sky shared any causal past. Yet the CMB has the same temperature in all directions to one part in 100,000, so the uniformity must be assumed rather than explained.
concepts.notes: GA draws it on a Penrose diagram; SCH poses it for nucleosynthesis-era uniformity. "Causal connection" (received from special-relativity) is folded in as the notion the problem turns on.

concepts.title: Flatness problem
concepts.summary: In a decelerating universe the departure of the total density parameter from one grows with time (as t for radiation, t^(2/3) for matter), so a universe near critical density today must have started absurdly close to it. The problem is to explain this tuning rather than impose it as an initial condition.
concepts.notes: GA states the growth of |Omega - 1| without proof; DIV derives it from |1 - rho/rho_crit| = |k|/(aH)^2.

concepts.title: Cosmic inflation
concepts.summary: A proposed very early phase, around 10^-35 s, of nearly exponential expansion driven by a large temporary vacuum-like energy. It inflates a small causally connected patch beyond our observable universe, solving the horizon problem, drives any spatial curvature to negligible values so the density parameter approaches one, and turns quantum fluctuations into the seeds of structure.

names: dilution of spatial curvature by inflation

merged_from: dilution of spatial curvature by inflation
concepts.notes: The flattening argument (GA ch41: the curvature term k/adot^2 shrinks as adot grows, so cosh and sinh solutions approach the flat exponential) is folded in. SCH classes inflation as a model rather than a theory until its fields are identified; credited to Starobinsky, Guth and Linde.

concepts.title: Inflaton field
concepts.summary: The hypothetical, nearly uniform scalar field whose potential energy dominates the early universe and drives inflation; in a Robertson-Walker background it obeys phi-double-dot + 3H phi-dot + dV/dphi = 0. Its energy density is the kinetic term plus the potential and its pressure the kinetic term minus the potential, so a field dominated by potential energy acts like a temporary cosmological constant.

names: scalar field equation in an expanding universe

merged_from: scalar field equation in an expanding universe
concepts.notes: GA models it as a phi^4 field with a temperature-dependent mass term and warns it is not the Higgs field; DIV derives the field equation and stress tensor from a Lagrangian (signature +---). The field equation (GA ch41, boxed as a key equation of inflation) is folded in; the 3H phi-dot damping term is registered as hubble-friction in cosmological-dynamics.

concepts.title: Slow-roll inflation
concepts.summary: On a sufficiently flat stretch of potential, Hubble friction makes the field's acceleration and kinetic energy negligible, so 3H phi-dot is approximately -dV/dphi and the expansion rate is set by the nearly constant potential energy. The universe then expands almost exponentially until the field reaches the steep part of the potential.

concepts.title: End of inflation and reheating
concepts.summary: Inflation ends when the field's kinetic energy becomes comparable to its potential energy, typically as it falls into its minimum and oscillates. Couplings to other fields then convert that energy into particles and radiation, refilling the cold, empty post-inflation universe and starting the standard hot big bang.

names: conversion of vacuum energy to particles

concepts.notes: GA notes that a field resting at a positive-energy minimum would inflate forever.

concepts.title: Primordial density perturbations from inflation
concepts.summary: Quantum fluctuations of the inflaton are stretched to cosmic scales during inflation and become classical density perturbations with a nearly scale-invariant spectrum. They later appear as CMB anisotropies and seed galaxies, and the measured spectrum constrains the shape of the inflaton potential.

concepts.title: Primordial gravitational waves
concepts.summary: Gravitational waves produced in the very early universe, for example amplified from vacuum fluctuations during inflation, which travel almost unaffected except for redshift. They could be detected directly by future detectors or indirectly through B-mode polarization of the CMB, and their energy density is bounded by nucleosynthesis.
concepts.notes: Detection strategy and detector bands for stochastic backgrounds belong to gravitational-wave-astronomy.

concepts.title: E-mode and B-mode polarization
concepts.summary: A CMB polarization map splits into a curl-free, gradient-like part (E modes) and a curl-like part (B modes). Scalar density perturbations produce only E modes, while gravitational waves produce both, so primordial B modes would be a clean signature of gravitational waves at decoupling, though foreground dust and lensing also make B modes.
